meta.title: Ask the Mates Anything | MOONSHOTS AMA #289
meta.speakers: Peter Diamandis, Alex Wissner-Gross (AWG), Dave Blundin, Salim Ismail
meta.thread_line: 6 threads · can AI out-think its own training data, what replaces LLMs, BCI/disability breakthroughs, the AI-era playbook for data-sales/hardware-funding/career reinvention, overregulation as the real AI risk, and institutions breaking before abundance arrives

snapshot: Live audience AMA with Peter Diamandis and his three "Moonshot Mates": Alex Wissner-Gross (an AI/ASI researcher), Dave Blundin (VC), and Salim Ismail (exponential-organizations author) — no fixed topic, just caller questions.

Alex argues AI can already discover genuinely new physics (citing the reported Navier-Stokes solve) and that human-inherited "self-limiting beliefs" in training data are not a real ceiling — there are training approaches ("AXY"-class superbayesian methods) that avoid human priors entirely.
On what comes after LLMs: Alex says next-token prediction has "effectively infinite" runway; Dave expects the compute substrate to shift to photonics within roughly 18 months to two years.

Multiple callers got concrete, personal tactical advice: how to sell decades of proprietary industry data to AI labs, how 18-year-old hardware founders should pitch VCs, and how a mid-career professional with a mortgage should use AI to build side income without quitting their job.
Alex says the real AI risk right now is overregulation, not underregulation — he's "deathly concerned" the US could lose a superintelligence race with China by regulating too early.

Peter frames the current moment as roughly 20 simultaneous "Gutenberg moments" hitting ~50 core institutions (healthcare, education, law, democracy) at once, with a 10-20 year adjustment window and a flagged 2-8 year risk of civil unrest.

BCI (brain-computer interface) comes up repeatedly — as a near-term disability breakthrough, as a general human-augmentation path, and as one of two interfaces (personalized-AI-filter, BCI) the mates think will reshape how humans process information.
Sponsor segments (Abundance Summit/Link Ventures intro, Google for Startups, Blitzy, and a Fountain Life-branded heart-disease segment) are excluded from this brief per standing policy.

themes.title: Can AI out-think the human biases baked into its own training data?
themes.lead: A caller asked whether AI could be trained to escape human self-limiting beliefs entirely, and Alex Wissner-Gross's answer doubled as a case for AI already discovering new physics.
bullets: Caller Griff proposed training separate AI models to inhabit and rigorously test radically different ontologies (deterministic universes, block-universe models, information-first physics, alternative quantum-mechanics interpretations) without ever telling them which is "true."

Alex's read: current models inherit humans' self-limiting beliefs because they're trained on human data, but points to a specific class of algorithms — "AXY"-style training for **superbayesian intelligences** — built to approach a universal prior with no human inductive bias baked in at all.
Alex: "I don't think that any inductive priors present in pre-training data will somehow hamstring AI's ability to make new scientific discoveries that challenge dogma. Not at all concerned."

His evidence: this is already being tested via **prediction markets and forecasting benchmarks** that give AI systems only information up to a fixed cutoff time and score their predictions of real future events, science, and breakthroughs against what actually happens.

Navier-Stokes is the live example cited: a fluid-dynamics problem mathematicians had failed to crack, reportedly solved this week by 10,000 AI agents working in parallel for 88 hours — used here as proof AI discovery isn't capped by human priors.

On consciousness (separate caller, Ramani): Alex frames it as a "century problem," citing two live theories — consciousness as an emergent property of complexity (AI could get there) versus a top-down "localized antenna" model where consciousness is something minds *connect into* rather than generate; growing evidence tilts him toward the latter, but he says AI could in principle tune into that phenomenon too.

quote.text: I don't think this is a real issue.
quote.cite: — Alex Wissner-Gross, on whether human training-data bias will limit AI's scientific discovery

themes.watch: This is Alex's own confident framing of frontier AI-research debates that are genuinely unresolved in the field — he says himself that even defining "consciousness" rigorously enough to answer the question is likely 5+ years away.

themes.title: What replaces LLMs — and does AI-driven chip/energy efficiency solve the power bottleneck?
themes.lead: Two callers asked variations of "what's the next S-curve" — one about model architecture, one about energy — and got a shared answer: today's building blocks stick around, just get faster and cheaper.
bullets: Alex distinguishes LLMs (the language-modeling task: predicting the next word/token/bit) from transformers (the current architecture) — he expects the self-supervised next-token-prediction *task* to have "effectively infinite longevity" and to scale all the way to "solving everything," no successor task needed.

Dave's structural read on transformers: the MLP layer is functionally the same math as 20-30 years ago and isn't going anywhere; the residual connection ("residual superhighway") is newer but stable; attention itself — which he describes as closer to a notebook keeping running notes than a brain function — is the piece most likely to get radically restructured.

Dave's timeline: **compute substrate moves to photonics** next, and once physics itself gets reinvented by AI, possibly to something faster still — all within roughly **18 months to 2 years** by his estimate.

On energy (separate caller, Haley, asking if AI-designed chips reduce Nvidia dependency and cut compute's energy footprint): Alex says yes to efficiency gains, but stresses this is *also* about growing the absolute energy supply, not just using less per gigaflop — AI is already being used to optimize both sides.

Alex expects the world to be "well into our post-fusion era" within the next 10 years, with AI itself helping invent the breakthrough energy sources that come after fusion — not necessarily tied to any one company's approach (a caller asked specifically about Elon Musk's Dyson swarm plans; Alex expects other, independent Dyson swarms and post-fusion breakthroughs too).

quote.text: I am 100% sure that the compute substrate is going to move to photonics.

themes.watch: Both the 18-months-to-2-years architecture timeline and the 10-year post-fusion call are personal estimates offered live on the show, not published research.

themes.title: BCI as the near-term unlock for disability — and eventually for everyone
themes.lead: Two separate callers — one asking about cognitive "bandwidth," one asking about disability services — both got steered toward brain-computer interfaces as the answer.
bullets: Peter frames two coming "interfaces": (1) a personal AI that filters and summarizes information better than a person can for themselves, and (2) **BCI** — feeding pre-formed concepts (his example: the idea of a rabbit) directly into the brain rather than through language.

Peter discloses he is an investor/adviser to **three BCI companies** and says Ray Kurzweil personally introduced him to a fourth; he cites the brain's roughly 100 trillion synaptic connections / 100 billion neurons as the ceiling BCI is meant to extend, via what he calls a "third corpus callosum."
Alex and Salim expect BCI, full-dive VR, and human/non-human uploading to all **coexist** over the next few years rather than one replacing the others.

On disability (caller Rod, a retired psychiatric social worker): Alex tells the story of an MIT fraternity brother who broke his neck and became quadriplegic, typing with a pencil held in his mouth — Alex says AI today would let him build his own fully independent communication environment using only eyes and face.

Alex separately flags MIT's **H2O for Human** program as prior work on BCI for both disability and general human augmentation, and argues the exact same innovations enabling disability treatments (easier to get regulatory approval for) will spill over into augmentation for people without disabilities.

Peter's framing for anyone dealing with a genetic, medical, or neurodegenerative condition in their life: "there's no better time ever to be alive than now to have a chance to deal with it, potentially cure it, or at least augment."

themes.title: The AI-era playbook: sell your data, fund your hardware startup, reinvent mid-career
themes.lead: Three very different callers — a civil engineer, an 18-year-old drone founder, and a mid-career Midwest professional — got the same underlying advice: package what you have and make it trivially easy for someone else to say yes.
bullets: **Selling proprietary data to AI labs** (caller John, 40-year civil engineer with 30 years of full project records): Dave says labs including Mero, Scale, and OpenAI are actively writing **$5-10M+ checks** to buy corporate data archives outright — but a *conversation* is more expensive for them than a check, so package the data as a due-diligence deal with your own price attached; they won't have time to negotiate and will just accept a confident number.

Dave's anecdote for getting past the wall of silence at a lab: **Kevin Weil** (former OpenAI chief product officer) interviewed there, got no callback for weeks, assumed he'd been passed over — then ran into Sam Altman on the street, who told him "just show up... it's chaos." Dave's takeaway: physically go to San Francisco and meet the person doing acquisitions face to face; a coffee-shop meeting massively raises the odds of a deal.

**Funding hardware as a young founder** (caller Pierce, 18, building autonomous construction drones): Dave says VCs are newly serious about hardware and now expect **bigger checks** and a fully gelled 2-3-person founding team going in; he'd pair Pierce with an industry co-investor (his own example: a real-estate/hotel owner interested in construction automation) rather than raise alone. His framing advice: think of yourself as "an intelligence company whose products happen to have atoms," not a hardware company.
Dave's fallback path for a founder who can't assemble that syndicate: join an existing funded rocket or drone company for 6-9 months to build a track record, then spin out.

**Mid-career reinvention without quitting your job** (caller Matt, Indiana): Dave's advice is to "build your own Skippy" (a personal AI agent) and hack on small AI-driven revenue ideas at night; he expects **10-100 franchise-style opportunities** this year specifically designed by AI labs for non-technical people to plug into. He also cites Drew Houston's line — "you become the average of the five people you spend the most time with" — as a reason to deliberately build a circle of 4-5 peers online around this, not just locally.

Concrete tools named: **mercor.com**, where you describe your domain expertise and the system tells you its market value; and, for a caller building a glamping resort business, Dave suggests using new models (Fable 5.1 or Astra) to "vibe up" a customer-facing app in a day rather than hiring a developer.

Salim's advice to a caller worried Australia is falling behind in AI: don't worry — being outside the US/Europe/Japan means you skip "unlearning 50 years of Harvard MBA thinking," and he recommends deliberately blocking off 10-20% of unscheduled time for experimentation, since "if you wait till you have spare time, you'll never catch up."

quote.text: Having a conversation is much more expensive than writing the check.

themes.title: Alex's real fear isn't AI risk — it's regulating AI too early
themes.lead: Asked how a federal employee should frame AI risk assessments, Alex reframed the whole question: the danger he actually worries about is overregulation itself.
bullets: Alex: "the risk at this point is overregulation, not under regulation... I am deathly concerned that we will overregulate our way into losing a superintelligence race with China."

His stated reasoning: more than **150,000 people die every day**, and he believes superintelligence-driven medicine is "probably the single best antidote" — so regulatory delay has a direct human cost, not just an economic one.

His prescription for actual risk mitigation (as distinct from new regulation): constant internal **red-teaming** (a standing team that thinks non-stop about offense), and using AI to cheaply pre-write documents on the top 10 most likely future threats, with your name on them, so you're the one who gets found when a crisis hits.

Peter's tactical add-on for anyone wanting policy influence: publicly declare yourself the go-to expert on one narrow, specific risk scenario before it happens — he cites **David Sacks** (All-In podcast) being pulled into the White House for a year, and a second podcast regular who declared himself the top expert on the China AI race and was pulled in as a UN/White House adviser ahead of a September 24 meeting (Alex declined to guess the caption-garbled name with confidence).

Alex's broader framing for why he's not alarmed day-to-day: the industry is already advancing through what he calls "defensive co-scaling" — AI rewriting insecure legacy code faster than new attack surface appears — which he sees as a reason to let industry self-correct rather than legislate first.

quote.text: I am deathly concerned that we will overregulate our way into losing a superintelligence race with China.

themes.watch: This is Alex's personal policy stance, stated directly to a caller who works in tech regulation — it's a minority position relative to most public AI-safety commentary and is presented here without a counter-voice from the panel.

themes.title: Institutions are breaking before abundance arrives, and school hasn't noticed yet
themes.lead: Two callers — one worried about a coming "period of pain," one horrified that kindergarten classrooms look unchanged since the 1960s — got tied together into one thesis: the old institutions can't survive this many simultaneous shocks, and education is the clearest example.
bullets: Peter's framework: roughly **50 core institutions** run the world (healthcare, education, law, IP, democracy), and none of them can survive what he calls **~20 simultaneous "Gutenberg moments"** — AI plus life-extension plus other shifts hitting at once — without being rebuilt from scarcity-era assumptions to abundance-era ones.

Peter's own uncertainty window: this turbulent period started roughly 5-10 years ago and he expects it to run **another 10-20 years**, with the explicit open question being whether society can minimize how deep the "trough" gets.

Dave separately flags a **2-8 year window of civil-unrest risk**, driven by his read that most revolutions come from young men who are angry about jobs, family formation, or cost of living — not necessarily rationally connected to AI itself — a thesis he says he wrote up on Substack.

Historical parallels offered as reassurance this pattern isn't new: the Cuban Missile Crisis/duck-and-cover era, FDR's "only thing we have to fear is fear itself," and 1500s panic over the printing press (feared to destroy memory, spread misinformation, and corrupt the young) — Salim: "same pattern, every single time we have major technological change."

On education (caller Patrick, a classroom educator): Salim says schools are still run on a 19th-century model, and the core problem is an "impedance mismatch" — a child with AI can learn in an hour what takes a full day in a classroom. His fix: stop training kids for **supply-side** careers (doctor, lawyer, engineer) chosen before demand exists, and instead start from a problem they care about (a *massive transformative purpose*), then backfill skills plus what he calls the **21st-century "six C's."**

Peter points to **TKS.world** (an overlay program for ages 13-18 he's personally involved with) and **Alpha School** (built by his friend McKenzie Price) as existing models doing this now, and cites Mark Twain — "there are two important days in your life: the day you were born, and the day you find out why" — as the guiding idea.

Salim ties this to Immad Mostaque's "sovereign agent" concept, floating whether every child should get their own persistent AI agent from age five — Peter calls this "the Young Primer" and points to Neal Stephenson's *Diamond Age* as the source vision; Salim's own EXO community (~50,000 people) is described as an early attempt at organizing people for this institutional transition, functioning like "a peace corps for the world."

quote.text: A child with an AI today in an hour can learn what they could learn sitting in a classroom for the whole day. That impedance mismatch will break the existing system.

themes.watch: The 10-20 year and 2-8 year windows are Peter and Dave's own working estimates, offered live rather than modeled forecasts.

takeaways.title: If you hold decades of unique domain data, package it as a priced, one-click deal for AI labs rather than waiting for them to negotiate — and consider showing up in person if emails stall.
Don't write off LLMs as near-obsolete — watch instead for the compute substrate itself shifting toward photonics over the next 18-24 months.
If you're building assistive or accessibility tech, look at BCI specifically — it's the near-term unlock the panel is most confident about, not a distant one.
If you want influence on a coming AI policy risk, publicly document and own one specific, narrow scenario before it happens rather than waiting to be asked.
Stop steering kids toward supply-side career paths chosen in advance — help them find a problem worth solving first, then work backward to the skills.
Mid-career professionals with real constraints (mortgage, family) should describe their full situation to an LLM and brainstorm monetizable side-projects on the margin, not quit outright.

risks: All four speakers recommend programs and communities they're personally affiliated with throughout (Fountain Life, TKS.world, Abundance 360, EXO, Moonshots Live) — treat those as founder endorsements, not independent reviews.

This is a live, unscripted call-in AMA: figures like "150,000 deaths per day," the 18-months-to-2-years photonics timeline, and the 10-20 year institutional-adjustment window are working estimates stated in conversation, not sourced from a report.
One caller's reference to another podcast guest who became a White House/UN adviser on the China AI race was too caption-garbled to name with confidence and was described rather than named directly.

Sponsor segments (Abundance Summit/Link Ventures, Google for Startups, Blitzy, and a Fountain Life-branded heart-disease segment) are excluded from this brief entirely per standing policy, even though the Fountain Life segment contained specific medical statistics.

other_news.title: Peter's own project, "Remember Me": AI agents interview an elderly parent across many sessions and turn their life story into a biography; he says the AI-generated avatars are close to convincing but "not quite there yet."

An audience member (Scott, a former deep-sea ROV operator in Louisiana) described pivoting his career into AI-data-center cooling engineering after roughly $250B in AI infrastructure investment landed in the state, citing its natural-gas advantage and contributing to open-source cooling research via opencompute.org.

An audience member (John Rean) built tugboatcaregiving.com after being moved by a prior episode; the panel's advice for reaching burned-out caregivers was to start with AI-assisted daily planning, not full automation.
Salim mentioned a community project building networked "nano-villages" in exurban areas — collectively-solving clusters modeled loosely on a kibbutz but explicitly designed not to be isolationist.

glossary.def: Artificial General Intelligence (human-level across domains) versus Artificial Superintelligence (beyond human level); the panel treats AGI as effectively arrived and frames most of this discussion around what comes after it.
Brain-computer interface — hardware that reads from or writes to the brain directly, discussed here both as a disability breakthrough and a general human-augmentation path.
Alex Wissner-Gross's term for a class of training algorithms aimed at building AI with as close to a universal prior as possible, without inheriting human-specific inductive biases.
Peter Diamandis's shorthand for a single technology shift big enough to force existing institutions to rebuild from scratch; he frames the current era as roughly 20 of these hitting simultaneously.
Salim Ismail's term (from his exponential-organizations work) for the large, meaningful problem an individual or organization orients around before backfilling the skills needed to pursue it.
Salim's shorthand for the set of 21st-century skills (referenced but not itemized on air) he argues should replace supply-side career training in schools.

Alex's term for the idea that AI-driven offense (e.g., cyberattacks) and AI-driven defense (e.g., rewriting vulnerable legacy code) advance together, which he cites as a reason to let the industry self-correct rather than pre-regulate.
